article_title: A Community Effort to Support the Transition from Pre-K to Kindergarten
citation: Spain, A.K., Ehrlich, S.B., Cowhy, J.R., Dasgupta, D.K., & Lockaby, T. (2018). A community effort to support the transition from pre-K to kindergarten. Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research and Chapin Hall at the University of Chicago. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: Co-design transition programs around key components rather than a structured curriculum, while communicating a consistent vision
description: The report finds that focusing on key components rather than a structured curriculum, and co-developing the program with rather than for teachers, allowed flexibility for practitioners. Teachers reported that "not having a transitions curriculum created important fl exibility to respond to teacher and student needs in local community context and across diverse educational settings," and as co-designers they felt the common classroom practices aligned with student needs. The report cautions that this flexible approach must also include communication of a consistent vision to support future engagement and participation.
requirements: Communication of a consistent vision for the program to support engagement and participation
constraints: Variation in perceptions of alignment with curricula, goals, and visions of schools and centers created implementation barriers for some teachers
target_learners: pre-K and kindergarten teachers implementing transition practices in diverse educational settings
target_learning_goals: classroom and community transition practices aligned to local student needs
examples: PKTP teachers co-designed the common classroom practices, developed content for family learning activities, and established priorities for their professional learning community.
key_sources: Spain, A.K., Ehrlich, S.B., Cowhy, J.R., Dasgupta, D.K., & Lockaby, T. (2018). A community effort to support the transition from pre-K to kindergarten. Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research and Chapin Hall at the University of Chicago. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/community-effort-support-transition-pre-k-kindergarten

article_title: Kindergarten Entry Assessments: An Examination of Best Practices, National Trends, and Recommendations
citation: Rolla, A., Mottesi, G., Wylen, M., & Akinola, Y. (2024). Kindergarten Entry Assessments: An Examination of Best Practices, National Trends, and Recommendations. Region 15 Comprehensive Center at WestEd. https://wested.org/
title: Five-domain framework for high-quality kindergarten entry assessments
description: The brief defines a high-quality KEA as an assessment whose content spans five child development domains designed to gather comprehensive student data: "physical well-being, social–emotional skills, learning approaches, language and literacy, and cognitive development." It uses this framework as the core content criterion for KEA quality, alongside clear administration guidelines and alignment with curriculum standards and other early childhood assessments. The framework is attributed to prior work by the K–3 Formative Assessment Consortium, Weisenfeld and colleagues, and Yun and colleagues.
requirements: Content must encompass the five developmental domains to gather comprehensive student data
constraints: The brief presents this as a characteristic of high-quality KEAs drawn from cited prior work, not as a tested result of its own
target_learning_goals: comprehensive assessment of developmental progress across physical, social-emotional, learning-approach, language and literacy, and cognitive domains
examples: State and national KEAs listed in the brief's appendix table are described against these domains, including language, literacy, math, science, executive function, and social-emotional skills for state KEAs
key_sources: Rolla, A., Mottesi, G., Wylen, M., & Akinola, Y. (2024). Kindergarten Entry Assessments: An Examination of Best Practices, National Trends, and Recommendations. Region 15 Comprehensive Center at WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED673515

article_title: Kindergarten Entry Assessments: An Examination of Best Practices, National Trends, and Recommendations
citation: Rolla, A., Mottesi, G., Wylen, M., & Akinola, Y. (2024). Kindergarten Entry Assessments: An Examination of Best Practices, National Trends, and Recommendations. Region 15 Comprehensive Center at WestEd. https://wested.org/
title: Do not use KEA data for accountability, kindergarten-entry delay, or disability diagnosis
description: The brief states that although KEAs serve many purposes, certain uses are inappropriate: "KEA data should not be used as part of an accountability system for students, teachers, or early learning providers." It further advises that KEAs should not be used to delay a student's kindergarten start or to diagnose a learning disability. The principle bounds appropriate KEA use to instructional guidance and planning rather than high-stakes or diagnostic decisions.
requirements: KEA use should be matched to a state's specific intended purpose, since a KEA cannot meet all possible uses simultaneously
constraints: Evaluating programs with a KEA depends on the presence of a dedicated study designed for that purpose
target_learning_goals: appropriate use of assessment data to support learning rather than for accountability or diagnosis
examples: The brief directs readers to Table 1 in the Appendix, which details potential KEA uses at classroom, building or site, district, and state levels, marking evaluation uses as requiring a dedicated study
key_sources: Rolla, A., Mottesi, G., Wylen, M., & Akinola, Y. (2024). Kindergarten Entry Assessments: An Examination of Best Practices, National Trends, and Recommendations. Region 15 Comprehensive Center at WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED673515

article_title: Kindergarten Entry Assessments: An Examination of Best Practices, National Trends, and Recommendations
citation: Rolla, A., Mottesi, G., Wylen, M., & Akinola, Y. (2024). Kindergarten Entry Assessments: An Examination of Best Practices, National Trends, and Recommendations. Region 15 Comprehensive Center at WestEd. https://wested.org/
title: Tiered uses of KEA data across classroom, building, district, and state levels
description: The brief organizes potential KEA uses by interest-holder level in an appendix table adapted from Garver and Yun and colleagues. At the classroom level, uses include tailoring individualized instruction and engaging families; at the building level, shaping schoolwide programming and tracking students in a data management system; at the district level, measuring curriculum effectiveness and informing resource allocation; and at the state level, evaluating progress toward state goals and allocating funding. Uses marked with an asterisk require a dedicated evaluation study.
requirements: Uses at district and state levels for evaluating program impact require a dedicated study with the purpose of evaluation
constraints: KEAs cannot serve all of these purposes simultaneously
target_learning_goals: guiding instruction, programming, resource allocation, and progress monitoring from KEA data
examples: Classroom-level uses listed include identifying students requiring targeted services and creating a school readiness plan for each child
key_sources: Rolla, A., Mottesi, G., Wylen, M., & Akinola, Y. (2024). Kindergarten Entry Assessments: An Examination of Best Practices, National Trends, and Recommendations. Region 15 Comprehensive Center at WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED673515

article_title: High-Quality Early Childhood Assessment: Learning from States' Use of Kindergarten Entry Assessments
citation: Yun, C., Melnick, H., & Wechsler, M. (2021). High-quality early childhood assessment: Learning from states' use of kindergarten entry assessments. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/high-quality-kea
title: Three-component framework for high-quality, equitable kindergarten entry assessments: content, administration, and validity
description: The report organizes research and policy recommendations on early childhood assessment into three components. A high-quality KEA should 'have content that effectively measures essential developmental domains in ways that are developmentally appropriate and culturally relevant and can be connected to a system of ongoing formative assessment across p–3,' have administration procedures that are practical and fair for all young children, and yield results that are accurate for all children assessed. The framework is summarized in Table 1 as guiding considerations for choosing high-quality KEAs and draws on recommendations from the National Research Council, CEELO, NIEER, NAEYC, CCSSO, and other bodies.
requirements: KEA content must align with developmentally appropriate kindergarten standards, curricula, and instruction and be based on a learning progression
constraints: An assessment that measures only discrete reading or numeracy skills is not appropriate as a KEA
target_learning_goals: whole child development across social-emotional, cognitive, language and literacy, mathematical and scientific reasoning, and physical domains
examples: Table 1 lists guiding considerations under the Content, Administration, and Validity components
key_sources: Yun, C., Melnick, H., & Wechsler, M. (2021). High-quality early childhood assessment: Learning from states' use of kindergarten entry assessments. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/high-quality-kea

article_title: High-Quality Early Childhood Assessment: Learning from States' Use of Kindergarten Entry Assessments
citation: Yun, C., Melnick, H., & Wechsler, M. (2021). High-quality early childhood assessment: Learning from states' use of kindergarten entry assessments. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/high-quality-kea
title: Elements of high-quality KEA implementation: stakeholder involvement, purposeful communication, local flexibility, dedicated staffing, and gradual phase-in
description: From cross-state implementation analysis, the report finds that 'States and districts support KEA implementation and continuous improvement by involving multiple stakeholders, communicating about the KEA's purpose and use, and allowing for local flexibility.' Georgia prominently labels its KEA a formative tool, Illinois proactively briefs reporters, Colorado offers districts a menu of assessments, and Illinois permits a longer optional version. States and districts also maintain at least one staff position responsible for KEA oversight, professional development, data reporting, and resources, and implementation is supported by a gradual phase-in, adequate funding, and ongoing improvement processes.
requirements: At least one staff position responsible for KEA oversight, professional development, data reporting, and KEA resources
target_learners: kindergarten children and early elementary students
target_learning_goals: developmentally appropriate instruction informed by KEA data
examples: Figure 9 depicts elements of high-quality implementation of early childhood assessments
key_sources: Yun, C., Melnick, H., & Wechsler, M. (2021). High-quality early childhood assessment: Learning from states' use of kindergarten entry assessments. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/high-quality-kea

article_title: Advancing Achievement through Biliteracy. Brief #2: State Policy Levers to Support a Strong and Sustainable Bilingual Teacher Workforce in California
citation: Grayson, D., & Jacobson, A. (2026). Advancing achievement through biliteracy: Brief #2: State policy levers to support a strong and sustainable bilingual teacher workforce in California. WestEd. https://WestEd.org
title: Kern County regional BLA workforce planning pilot
description: A regional BLA workforce planning pilot that "brought together county, district, and educator preparation program partners in Kern County for a series of planning workshops in 2025 to examine recruitment and retention data and identify workforce strategies." The pilot is presented alongside the EL-WIN initiative as a scalable, replicable proof point demonstrating how districts, counties, and preparation programs can jointly analyze and coordinate supply and demand to address critical workforce needs.
requirements: Partnership among county offices, districts, and educator preparation programs; internal collection of workforce data where state systems do not provide it
constraints: The pilot county office of education collects some data only for some districts, and pilot districts have varied internal collection practices
target_learners: Multilingual Learners in Kern County bilingual instructional programs
target_learning_goals: expanding access to bilingual instructional programs that improve student achievement
examples: The pilot's workshops in 2025 examined recruitment and retention data and produced workforce strategies for strengthening the BLA workforce.

article_title: The Path to Conversational AI Tutors: Integrating Tutoring Best Practices and Targeted Technologies to Produce Scalable AI Agents
citation: Kirk Vanacore, Ryan S. Baker, Avery H. Closser, and Jeremy Roschelle. (2026). The Path to Conversational AI Tutors: Integrating Tutoring Best Practices and Targeted Technologies to Produce Scalable AI Agents. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.19303
title: Keep, Change, Center, Study framework for designing conversational AI tutors
description: A four-part design framework for conversational AI tutoring systems. It directs designers to keep evidence-based legacy ITS features (knowledge tracing, behavior and affect detection, knowledge graphs), change delivery by leveraging generative AI for automatic content generation and dialogic feedback, center opportunities unique to conversational tutoring (meaning-making, student agency, diagnosis of reasoning), and study open research questions (efficacy testing, student experience, human-AI collaboration). The article presents it as a research agenda for building tutors that are "scalable, pedagogically effective, and responsive to the social and motivational dimensions of learning".
requirements: Design must integrate legacy ITS learner-model technologies with generative AI rather than replacing them
constraints: The article states there is little evidence that generative AI alone can match the multifaceted nature of high-quality tutoring
target_learners: K-12 and higher-education students using conversational AI tutoring systems
target_learning_goals: Conceptual learning supported by dialogue-based tutoring, including motivation and self-regulation
examples: Table 1 summarizes the four categories with examples such as knowledge tracing for Keep and automatic content generation for Change
key_sources: Kirk Vanacore, Ryan S. Baker, Avery H. Closser, and Jeremy Roschelle. (2026). The Path to Conversational AI Tutors: Integrating Tutoring Best Practices and Targeted Technologies to Produce Scalable AI Agents. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.19303

article_title: Experiences, appearances, and interprofessional training: The instructional use of video in post-simulation debriefings
citation: Elin Johansson, Oskar Lindwall, Hans Rystedt. (2017). Experiences, appearances, and interprofessional training: The instructional use of video in post-simulation debriefings. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-017-9252-z
title: Selecting short clips of successful 'key events' as the debriefing focus
description: The facilitators typically selected one short clip (approximately one to three minutes in length) of a situation in which the students successfully performed actions included in the learning goals. The clip was introduced in the analysis phase with the facilitator saying something about the aspects of teamwork on which students were expected to focus, and the rationale for the positive focus was to make students aware of successful actions "so that they could maintain those as they entered their future professional practices".
requirements: A stated pedagogical rationale framing what students should focus on when watching
Video capture of the scenario with multiple cameras
constraints: Except for a few occasions when the technology did not work properly, clips were used in all 40 debriefings
target_learners: final-year medical and nursing students in mixed interprofessional groups of 4–8
target_learning_goals: identifying and assessing well-functioning teamwork and communication practices
examples: Clips exemplifying SBAR-reporting, speak up, or closed loop communication were shown and discussed

article_title: Why We Might Still be Concerned About Low Cronbach’s Alphas in Domain-specific Knowledge Tests
citation: Steffen Zitzmann, Gabe A. Orona. (2025). Why We Might Still be Concerned About Low Cronbach's Alphas in Domain-specific Knowledge Tests. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10015-5
title: Keep well justified alpha thresholds as rough guidelines rather than abandoning them, and view a low alpha as a threat rather than a sign of validity
description: Against the recommendation to drop alpha thresholds, the authors argue that "a well justified threshold can be a valuable means if it is understood as a rough guideline to achieve a level of reliability that is high enough to prevent most of the discussed adverse effects on results." They contend that interpreting a low alpha as indicating content validity could be exploited to legitimate low reliability, and that a high alpha remains an important prerequisite for research and individual diagnostics. Developers should opt for a balanced strategy rather than playing reliability off against validity.
requirements: Thresholds must be well justified and understood as rough guidelines, and interval estimates should accompany the point estimate when applying them.
constraints: The authors acknowledge a threshold can be misused in ways that increase the file drawer problem or reduce the content validity of tests.
target_learning_goals: Maintaining reliability of domain-specific knowledge test scores for research and individual assessment
examples: The commentary argues that viewing a low alpha as a feature of knowledge tests unintentionally provides an argument other authors could exploit to play down or legitimate a low alpha.
key_sources: Steffen Zitzmann, Gabe A. Orona. (2025). Why We Might Still be Concerned About Low Cronbach's Alphas in Domain-specific Knowledge Tests. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10015-5

article_title: Some observations on the learning of sensible material.
citation: Dell, John A. (1911). Some Observations on the Learning of Sensible Material. Journal of Educational Psychology, 2, 401-406.
title: Do not alter the natural sequence of lesson facts to exploit primacy or recency, because other causes of remembering dominate position
description: The article draws a practical recommendation from its three experiments: although "the beginning and the end of a lesson are the best places for facts which have to be remembered" other things being equal, for rational material other things are generally not equal. Since recall depends on associations by similarity with prior knowledge rather than on serial position, "it is not worth while to alter the natural sequence of the facts in order to bring any particular fact to the beginning or end". Teachers should preserve the logical order of meaningful content instead of reordering it for position effects.
requirements: Applies to sensible material whose facts bear a rational relation to one another; meaningless series behave differently
constraints: The recommendation rests on classroom experiments with schoolboys and on the author's interpretation, not on a direct test of reordering outcomes
target_learning_goals: retention of meaningful lesson and lecture content
examples: The bud lesson was actually taught to two forms with its three groups of facts in different orders, and the reordering made no difference to which section was best remembered
key_sources: Dell, John A. (1911). Some Observations on the Learning of Sensible Material. Journal of Educational Psychology, 2, 401-406. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0074801

article_title: A study of association in defectives.
citation: Otis, M. (1915). A Study of Association in Defectives. The Journal of Educational Psychology, Vol. VI, No. 5. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22A+Study+of+Association+in+Defectives%22+Otis
title: Kent-Rosanoff 100-word association list with standardized frequency tables
description: The Kent-Rosanoff list of 100 stimulus words is a standardized word-association instrument with published frequency tables providing "a standard of comparison in the frequency tables published at the close of their work." Otis used it so that "a comparison with normal reactions could be made," administering the words individually in list order with stop-watch timing. Normal-type (Type V) responses were scored against the Kent-Rosanoff frequency tables, and new frequency tables compiled from the defectives and normal school children were placed on file at the Vineland laboratory.
requirements: Individual administration in a private room with a reliable stop-watch, recording responses verbatim and timing in tenths of seconds.
constraints: Some list words are beyond the comprehension of very young children, though the author judges enough words are adapted to a child's understanding to make the test fair.
target_learning_goals: assessment of associational tendencies and mental status
examples: Frequency tables compiled from the defectives' and normal children's responses were placed on file at the Vineland laboratory for consultation.
key_sources: Otis, M. (1915). A Study of Association in Defectives. The Journal of Educational Psychology, Vol. VI, No. 5. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22A+Study+of+Association+in+Defectives%22+Otis

article_title: A constructive ability test.
citation: Kelley, Truman Lee. (1916). A constructive ability test. The Journal of Educational Psychology, Vol. VII, No. 1. https://www.google.com/search?q=Kelley+1916+A+Constructive+Ability+Test+Journal+of+Educational+Psychology
title: The Constructive Ability Test: block-building task with four design criteria and a structured record blank
description: A test in which the child is given blocks and instructed in his native tongue "to build the best thing he can and whatever he chooses", so that the end is not set by the examiner. It was designed to meet four criteria: to be free from dependence upon language, free from preceding formal training, to test initiative as well as manipulative ability, and to be capable of objective grading and standardization. Administration uses a time limit of twice as many minutes as the child is years old, and a record blank scoring purpose, dominance of purpose, symmetry, interest in building versus playing, and merit of each successive structure.
requirements: A set of limited building material as shown in Plate I, a trained grader, and the 40-sample stereoscopic photograph scale for merit grading
constraints: Structures incomplete because of lack of material are not graded as high as structures incomplete because of lack of time
Time may be a trifle short for adults around twenty years of age
The norms so far drawn up rest on boys, so if high-school boys differ from boys in general they would be those of a select group
target_learners: exceptional children (twice the mental age allowed)
target_learning_goals: constructive and executive ability
initiative in setting one's own task
manipulative ability
examples: Children are asked at sixty seconds what they are going to build, and graded excellent=5 to no purpose=0 for dominance of purpose
A large wheel is included in the material as a distraction that suggests playing, to observe interest in building versus aimless play
key_sources: Kelley, Truman Lee. (1916). A constructive ability test. The Journal of Educational Psychology, Vol. VII, No. 1. https://www.google.com/search?q=Kelley+1916+A+Constructive+Ability+Test+Journal+of+Educational+Psychology

article_title: On opportunities and challenges of large multimodal foundation models in education
citation: Küchemann, S., Avila, K. E., Dinc, Y., Hortmann, C., Revenga, N., Ruf, V., Stausberg, N., Steinert, S., Fischer, F., Fischer, M., Kasneci, E., Kasneci, G., Kuhr, T., Kutyniok, G., Malone, S., Sailer, M., Schmidt, A., Stadler, M., Weller, J. & Kuhn, J. (2025). On opportunities and challenges of large multimodal foundation models in education. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00301-w
title: Keep the human in the loop: treat LMFMs as supplementary tools that complement rather than replace human teaching
description: The review's concluding design principle is that AI must complement rather than replace human teachers, developers, and researchers, who remain central to understanding, communicating, and mitigating LMFM risks. It states that "Emphasizing AI as a supplementary tool in teaching is paramount, ensuring it complements rather than replaces human teaching", and that researchers should view AI as a supportive tool enhancing rather than substituting the indispensable skills they contribute. The principle applies across learners, educators, researchers, and developers.
requirements: Awareness among students and educators of LMFM challenges and risks for effective integration and risk mitigation.
Human oversight to verify output accuracy and trace sources.
constraints: The review warns of a risk of developing an overreliance on LMFMs, creating a dependency that could leave researchers ill-equipped without AI support; it also notes human skills must be decided upon for curriculum retention or reduction.
target_learning_goals: responsible and ethical AI integration in education
preservation of human competencies alongside AI-supported learning
examples: The review concludes that LMFMs should be understood as tools enabling interactive, tailored, and efficient educational environments that teachers and students can personalize without programming skills, while keeping the human in the loop as a responsible teacher or increasingly self-directed learner.

article_title: An Intelligent Tutoring System for Entity Relationship Modelling
citation: Pramuditha Suraweera, Antonija Mitrovic. (2004). An Intelligent Tutoring System for Entity Relationship Modelling. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00197310
title: KERMIT: a problem-solving environment for practising conceptual database design with the Entity-Relationship data model
description: KERMIT is a "Knowledge-based Entity Relationship Modelling Intelligent Tutor" described as "a problem-solving environment for the university-level students, in which they can practise conceptual database design using the Entity-Relationship data model". The system observes students' actions, adapts to their knowledge and learning abilities, and was deployed within genuine teaching activities in database courses.
requirements: University-level students practising conceptual database design with the Entity-Relationship data model
target_learning_goals: conceptual database design using the Entity-Relationship data model
examples: The paper describes the system's architecture and functionality and evaluates it in the context of genuine teaching activities.

article_title: Early prediction of writing quality using keystroke logging
citation: Rianne Conijn, Christine Cook, Menno van Zaanen, Luuk Van Waes. (2022). Early prediction of writing quality using keystroke logging. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00268-w
title: Five-category taxonomy of keystroke features for writing-process analysis
description: The article organizes keystroke-log features drawn from prior literature into five groups: "features related to timings of pauses, revisions, typing bursts, verbosity, and other (non-typing) events". Pause features include IKI metrics and long-pause percentages; revision features cover backspaces and leading-edge versus in-text revisions; fluency features capture bursts; verbosity features count keystrokes and words plus 30-s variability measures; other-event features include focus shifts and cut/paste/jump durations. The study extracted 54 features in these categories from Inputlog raw logs for prediction modeling.
requirements: Keystroke logs with per-keystroke event records, plus a baseline copy task to set individual pause and IKI thresholds, as the article required for feature extraction.
constraints: The authors state keystroke logging data are indirect observation, so they make no theoretical claims about cognitive subprocesses; their approach is explicitly data-driven.
target_learners: ESL students in higher education academic writing courses
target_learning_goals: Academic summarization and writing quality
examples: 54 features were extracted from raw Inputlog logs of a 30-minute timed academic summary task written by 126 ESL premaster students.
key_sources: Rianne Conijn, Christine Cook, Menno van Zaanen, Luuk Van Waes. (2022). Early prediction of writing quality using keystroke logging. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00268-w

article_title: Implementing CBM: SQL-Tutor After Fifteen Years
citation: Mitrovic, A., & Ohlsson, S. (2015). Implementing CBM: SQL-Tutor After Fifteen Years. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0049-9
title: Bridge the theory-technology gap: keep talking across research and implementation communities
description: From the SQL-Tutor experience the authors draw the lesson that theoretical concepts and implementation efforts must be brought together deliberately. They write that "The first lesson of SQL-Tutor in particular and the CBM approach in general for ITS researchers is thus simple to state but sometimes hard to execute: Keep talking." Basic inquiry into cognitive skills and willingness of technologists to implement systems jointly revealed the weaknesses of bug-library tutoring and enabled the CBM alternative. They note institutional disincentives often get in the way of such gap-bridging.
requirements: Willingness of researchers on both sides of the theory-technology gap to reach out to each other
constraints: Institutional disincentives to gap-bridging all too often get in the way, per the authors
target_learning_goals: productive research and development of tutoring systems
examples: The two authors, one a theorist and one a system builder, collaborated after a 1998 sabbatical visit, producing SQL-Tutor and the CBM line of tutors
key_sources: Mitrovic, A., & Ohlsson, S. (2015). Implementing CBM: SQL-Tutor After Fifteen Years. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0049-9

article_title: Integrated Education Models for Addressing Substance Use Among Schoolchildren: A Scoping Review of School-Based Educational Interventions.
citation: Bajpai Tewari, D., Gautam, U., Jaiswal, V., Pooja, Mishra, A., & Das, P. (2026). Integrated Education Models for Addressing Substance Use Among Schoolchildren: A Scoping Review of School-Based Educational Interventions. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph23081073
title: keepin' it R.E.A.L. (kiR) resistance-skills curriculum
description: The keepin' it R.E.A.L. model teaches resistance strategies — Refusal, Explain, Avoid, Leave — "based on the premise that most children who initiate substance use at an early age do so not out of the desire to try it, but because they lack the requisite social skills to resist drug offers." It comprises 10 interactive classroom sessions, five videos scripted, acted and filmed by students, and booster activities after every session. Seven of the review's 43 studies examined its efficacy, including acculturation, entertainment-education and cross-national Mexican variants.
requirements: Delivery through interactive classroom sessions with accompanying videos and booster activities, as printed in Table 3.
constraints: Review-synthesised kiR outcomes varied across variants: original kiR showed no significant behavioural change in one trial, and the Acculturation Enhancement version increased substance use expectancies by 8th grade.
target_learners: Middle-school students (5th-8th grade in the reviewed kiR studies)
target_learning_goals: Drug-offer refusal, resistance skills, refusal self-efficacy, decision-making, and anti-drug expectancies
examples: The review describes 10 interactive classroom sessions, five student-scripted videos, and booster activities after every classroom session.
key_sources: Bajpai Tewari, D., Gautam, U., Jaiswal, V., Pooja, Mishra, A., & Das, P. (2026). Integrated Education Models for Addressing Substance Use Among Schoolchildren: A Scoping Review of School-Based Educational Interventions. article_title: Determining the metrics of competence in robotic hysterectomy: a systematic review.
citation: Arcamo K, Murugappan S, Larkins K, Mohan H, Costello A, Pendlebury A, McNally O, McBain R. (2025). Determining the metrics of competence in robotic hysterectomy: a systematic review. Journal of Robotic Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11701-025-02471-6
title: Kern's six-step framework for curriculum development structures the review's approach to informing robotic hysterectomy curriculum design.
description: The review is situated within a structured curriculum development effort at the International Medical Robotics Academy (IMRA) using Kern's six-step approach. The authors state that the steps "Goals And Objectives and Evaluation And Feedback" serve to identify specific and measurable objectives and opportunities for formative feedback. This review addresses those sections of Kern's framework by evaluating existing performance metrics for robotic hysterectomy. The framework provides the organizing rationale for why valid metrics are a prerequisite for an effective training curriculum.
requirements: A structured curriculum development process, such as Kern's six-step approach, to identify measurable objectives and feedback opportunities.
target_learning_goals: acquiring technical competence in robotic hysterectomy
key_sources: Arcamo K, Murugappan S, Larkins K, Mohan H, Costello A, Pendlebury A, McNally O, McBain R. (2025). Determining the metrics of competence in robotic hysterectomy: a systematic review. Journal of Robotic Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11701-025-02471-6

article_title: Education in the placement of ultrasound-guided peripheral venous catheters: a systematic review.
citation: Jørgensen Rasmus, Laursen Christian B., Konge Lars, Pietersen Pia Iben. (2021). Education in the placement of ultrasound-guided peripheral venous catheters: a systematic review. Scandinavian Journal of Trauma, Resuscitation and Emergency Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13049-021-00897-z
title: Kern's six-step model for curriculum development as an organizing framework for USG-PVC education
description: Kern's six-step model is a curriculum-development framework the review uses to structure its evaluation of existing USG-PVC education. The steps are "problem identification and general needs-assessment, targeted needs-assessment, setting goals and measurable objectives, educational strategies, implementation, and evaluation and feedback", with earlier steps revisited throughout. The review maps its findings onto these steps, finding needs assessments absent, curricula poorly described, and assessment tools rarely validity-tested.
requirements: Assessment tools preferably based on solid evidence of validity should be used to ensure the set goals and objectives
constraints: The review found no needs-assessment studies and a lack of defined curricula and competency-assurance tools in the included literature
target_learning_goals: competence in ultrasound-guided peripheral venous catheter placement
examples: The review used the model to evaluate existing knowledge: no needs-assessment studies were found, curricula generally included ultrasound physics, knobology, probe selection, vascular and nerve recognition, preparation, and complications, and only Primdahl's rating scale had explored validity evidence via Messick's framework
key_sources: Jørgensen Rasmus, Laursen Christian B., Konge Lars, Pietersen Pia Iben. (2021). Education in the placement of ultrasound-guided peripheral venous catheters: a systematic review. Scandinavian Journal of Trauma, Resuscitation and Emergency Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13049-021-00897-z

article_title: The Effect of Keyword Method on Vocabulary Retention of Senior High School EFL Learners in Iran
citation: Davoudi, M., & Yousefi, D. (2016). The Effect of Keyword Method on Vocabulary Retension of Senior High School EFL Learners in Iran. Journal of Education and Practice, 7(11). https://www.iiste.org
title: The keyword method as a mnemonic strategy linking new words to memorable associations
description: The keyword method is a mnemonic vocabulary-learning strategy in which learners associate a new L2 word with a memorable keyword, often an interactive image, to aid recall. The article defines mnemonics as "any procedure that facilitates recal l of pieces of new information" and explains the keyword method's success via visual stimuli and links between new information and learners' schemata. It situates the method within memory/consolidation strategies that relate words to previous knowledge.
requirements: Learners need explicit instruction in the strategy and opportunities to create their own corresponding keyword for each vocabulary item
constraints: The article notes elementary learners might not be able to learn or recall as efficiently as older learners do
target_learning_goals: vocabulary retention and recall of L2 words
examples: The experimental group was given a keyword method strategy study sheet and was required to help create a corresponding keyword for each vocabulary item in their own ways.
key_sources: Davoudi, M., & Yousefi, D. (2016). The Effect of Keyword Method on Vocabulary Retension of Senior High School EFL Learners in Iran. Journal of Education and Practice, 7(11). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1099563

article_title: The Effects of an Experiential Approach to Learning on Student Motivation
citation: Marshall A. Baker & J. Shane Robinson. (2017). The Effects of an Experiential Approach to Learning on Student Motivation. Journal of Agricultural Education, 58(3), 150-167. https://doi.org/10.5032/jae.2017.03150
title: Keller's ARCS Model of Motivation
description: The ARCS model is Keller's framework for designing motivating instruction, grounded in expectancy-value theory. "ARCS represent the four conceptual categories of motivation: (a) attention, (b) relevance, (c) confidence, and (d) satisfaction" — four conditions that must be present for people to become and remain motivated. The study used the model as its primary theoretical frame and measured motivation with the IMMS built on it, and recommends teachers use its process questions to embed motivation in instruction.
requirements: Instruction must be designed so the four motivational conditions — attention, relevance, confidence, and satisfaction — are present for learners to become and remain motivated.
target_learning_goals: student motivation to learn course content
examples: Both the experiential and direct instruction treatments in the study were carefully designed to meet the tenets of Keller's model, and both proved motivating.
key_sources: Marshall A. Baker & J. Shane Robinson. (2017). The Effects of an Experiential Approach to Learning on Student Motivation. Journal of Agricultural Education, 58(3), 150-167. https://doi.org/10.5032/jae.2017.03150

article_title: Impact of a Mnemonic Strategy on Learning Science Concepts for Middle School Students with Specific Learning Disabilities
citation: Aracı, N., Melekoğlu, M. A., & Çetin, M. E. (2023). Impact of a Mnemonic Strategy on Learning Science Concepts for Middle School Students With Specific Learning Disabilities. Learning Disabilities: A Contemporary Journal, 21(1), 69-85.
title: Keyword strategy: a three-stage mnemonic for learning science concepts
description: The keyword strategy is a mnemonic strategy first developed by Atkinson (1975) that consists of "an acoustic bond established between words and the steps of supporting this bond with visuals". Levin (1988) simplified it into three stages: saving (selecting a pronunciation-similar keyword), associating (linking the target word to the keyword via verbal repetition and an image), and retrieval (recalling the keyword and image to derive the target word's meaning). The article applies this strategy to teach ten Turkish science concepts to students with SLD.
requirements: Keywords must be acoustically similar to the target concept words in the learners' language
Visuals representing the keyword-concept association must be prepared
constraints: The article examines the strategy only for middle school students with SLD learning science concepts in Türkiye
target_learners: middle school students with specific learning disabilities
target_learning_goals: science concept acquisition and retention
examples: Ten Turkish science concepts were taught with keyword pairs such as globe–oar (küre–kürek) and ocean–dolphin (okyanus–yunus), with designer-prepared visuals
key_sources: Aracı, N., Melekoğlu, M. A., & Çetin, M. E. (2023). Impact of a Mnemonic Strategy on Learning Science Concepts for Middle School Students With Specific Learning Disabilities. Learning Disabilities: A Contemporary Journal, 21(1), 69-85. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1386167

article_title: Designing an antimicrobial stewardship curriculum for nurses to strengthen knowledge and clinical practice.
citation: Aldawood Fatima Dawood, Shamas Nour, Alshamrani Majid. (2026). Designing an antimicrobial stewardship curriculum for nurses to strengthen knowledge and clinical practice. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09314-4
title: Kern's six-step framework combined with a shared governance model guides nursing AMS curriculum development
description: The article uses Kern's six-step framework for healthcare curriculum design—problem identification, targeted needs assessment, goals and objectives, educational strategies, implementation, and evaluation and feedback—integrated with a shared governance model to guide the development of a nursing AMS curriculum. The authors state that "Combining the framework and model was necessary for shared decision-making and fostering responsibility and ownership among the departments involved in this initiative." Kern's framework guides implementation by considering factors influencing curriculum outcomes, while the shared governance model guides step-by-step planning by identifying key stakeholders, facilitators, and barriers.
requirements: Collaboration between the AMS team and nursing department leadership at multiple levels to enable shared decision-making
constraints: The steps are listed sequentially but were implemented non-sequentially using dynamic and interactive processes
target_learners: Registered nurses at a tertiary healthcare institution
target_learning_goals: Antimicrobial stewardship knowledge and clinical practice
examples: The AMS team met with top-level, middle-level, and first-line nursing leadership to form task forces and secure buy-in at each stage of curriculum development
key_sources: Aldawood Fatima Dawood, Shamas Nour, Alshamrani Majid. (2026). Designing an antimicrobial stewardship curriculum for nurses to strengthen knowledge and clinical practice. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09314-4

article_title: Design and implementation of a microlearning-based OSCE preparatory curriculum in obstetrics: a pilot study.
citation: Michlmayr N., Mitofsky J., Haverkamp N., Wittek A., Plöger R., Walter A., Strizek B., Recker F. (2025). Design and implementation of a microlearning-based OSCE preparatory curriculum in obstetrics: a pilot study. Archives of Gynecology and Obstetrics. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00404-025-08157-6
title: Kern's six-step approach to curriculum development as a framework for designing medical education tools
description: Kern's six-step approach is a widely used medical education framework comprising problem identification and general needs assessment, targeted needs assessment, formulation of goals and objectives, selection of educational strategies, implementation, and evaluation and feedback. The article used it as the organizing structure for building the MiLeMed curriculum, reporting one results section per step. It grounds design choices in assessed needs before strategy selection.
requirements: Sequentially addressing each step to ensure a structured and evidence-informed development process
target_learning_goals: Structured, evidence-informed curriculum design
examples: The article's Results section is organized by the six steps, from needs assessment through evaluation and feedback.
key_sources: Michlmayr N., Mitofsky J., Haverkamp N., Wittek A., Plöger R., Walter A., Strizek B., Recker F. (2025). Design and implementation of a microlearning-based OSCE preparatory curriculum in obstetrics: a pilot study. Archives of Gynecology and Obstetrics. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00404-025-08157-6

article_title: A Large-Scale Multispecialty Evaluation of Web-Based Simulation in Medical Microbiology Laboratory Education: Randomized Controlled Trial.
citation: Lei Xu, Xichuan Deng, Tingting Chen, Nan Lu, Yuran Wang, Jia Liu, Yanan Guo, Zeng Tu, Yuxin Nie, Yeganeh Hosseini, Yonglin He. (2025). A Large-Scale Multispecialty Evaluation of Web-Based Simulation in Medical Microbiology Laboratory Education: Randomized Controlled Trial. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/72495
title: Kern's 6-step curriculum development model applied as a closed-loop design framework for the virtual simulation system
description: The article structures its system development on Kern's 6-step curriculum development model, moving from problem identification and needs assessment through objective formulation, educational strategies, implementation, and evaluation. The design is described as embodying a closed-loop concept: interactive virtual microscopy addresses limited specimen types, the real-time feedback system corresponds to error-correction needs, and the automated assessment module enables both formative assessment and personalized learning curves supporting continuous curriculum improvement. The authors state this completely realizes a closed-loop curriculum development process from problem identification to effect evaluation.
requirements: A hierarchical competency framework established through needs assessment, here covering Gram staining, culture isolation, biochemical testing, and integrated diagnosis
target_learners: medical students in microbiology laboratory courses
target_learning_goals: standardized BSL-2 pathogen handling and cocci identification skills
examples: The system's basic modules implemented standardized aseptic operating procedures, intermediate modules integrated dynamic specimen generation, and advanced modules incorporated an embedded real-time assessment system
key_sources: Lei Xu, Xichuan Deng, Tingting Chen, Nan Lu, Yuran Wang, Jia Liu, Yanan Guo, Zeng Tu, Yuxin Nie, Yeganeh Hosseini, Yonglin He. (2025). A Large-Scale Multispecialty Evaluation of Web-Based Simulation in Medical Microbiology Laboratory Education: Randomized Controlled Trial. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/72495

article_title: Diabe-teach: a randomized controlled trial of a gamified approach to enhance medical undergraduates' knowledge and comprehension of diabetes mellitus.
citation: Mariam S, Heba I, Mohamed FHN. (2025). Diabe-teach: a randomized controlled trial of a gamified approach to enhance medical undergraduates’ knowledge and comprehension of diabetes mellitus. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06602-9
title: Keyword-chain board-game pattern: build and verbally justify connected chains of concept cards
description: A reusable session-level design in which topic keywords are laid out as a shuffled grid and learners construct chains of at least four connected terms, then explain the connections to peers with instructor feedback. The open-ended, “nontrivial” format “emphasizes on constructing meaningful connections between keywords, which fosters critical thinking,” and the shuffled dynamic board prevents predictability across sessions. The pattern combines active retrieval, peer explanation, and immediate instructor feedback in one face-to-face activity.
requirements: A curated keyword set aligned to learning objectives; learners with enough baseline familiarity to attempt connections; a facilitator to adjudicate ambiguous chains; timed rounds with a trial round to teach mechanics
constraints: Requires substantial session time (about 75 minutes of intervention in the reported study)
validation of chain correctness depends on group consensus and instructor judgment
target_learning_goals: Integrating and correlating key concepts across a complex topic
Communicating scientific reasoning to peers
examples: Diabe-teach sessions: 15-minute orientation/trial, then two 30-minute rounds in which the first 20 minutes were used to analyse the grid and form chains and the last 10 minutes to explain chains and receive feedback
key_sources: Mariam S, Heba I, Mohamed FHN. (2025). Diabe-teach: a randomized controlled trial of a gamified approach to enhance medical undergraduates’ knowledge and comprehension of diabetes mellitus. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06602-9

article_title: Effectiveness of the online-eLearning program KeepCoool at improving the vaccine cold chain in general practices.
citation: Thielmann Anika, Schmitz Marie-Therese, Welchowski Thomas, Weltermann Birgitta. (2024). Effectiveness of the online-eLearning program KeepCoool at improving the vaccine cold chain in general practices. PLoS ONE 19(4): e0301847. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0301847
title: KeepCoool: a guideline-based eLearning program on vaccine cold chain management for general practices
description: KeepCoool is a freely available best-practices-based eLearning program providing content in five tutorials: temperature, refrigerator, storage, responsibilities, and monitoring. It uses three didactic elements: "a) personal address, b) targeting of the respective profession (physicians or practice assistants), c) individualized feedback tailored to a participant's baseline knowledge". Participants complete an 11-item knowledge questionnaire at start, receive consistent presentation with basic information, tips for the practice, and expert knowledge, and earn a certificate after answering ≥ 7 of 11 questions correctly.
requirements: Participants need access to the online program; a certificate requires successfully answering at least 7 of 11 knowledge questions (> 60% correct answers as required by the regional physician association).
constraints: Content is based on recommendations from several countries (US, UK, Australia, Canada, Scotland) and was evaluated in German general practices.
target_learning_goals: vaccine cold chain maintenance
vaccine storage management knowledge
examples: In the study, 47 physicians and practice assistants from practices with cold chain breaches participated in the eLearning; the first person per practice finished the test on average 7.4 days after receiving login information.
key_sources: Thielmann Anika, Schmitz Marie-Therese, Welchowski Thomas, Weltermann Birgitta. (2024). Effectiveness of the online-eLearning program KeepCoool at improving the vaccine cold chain in general practices. PLoS ONE 19(4): e0301847. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0301847

article_title: Blended learning: ten tips on how to implement it into a curriculum in healthcare education.
citation: Hege I, Tolks D, Adler M, Härtl A. (2020). Blended learning: ten tips on how to implement it into a curriculum in healthcare education. GMS Journal for Medical Education 37(5): Doc45. https://www.egms.de/en/journals/zma/2020-37/zma001338.shtml
title: Plan blended learning curricula with the (adapted) six-step Kern cycle, planning revision early
description: The article recommends applying the six-step Kern cycle of curriculum development — problem identification, targeted needs assessment, goals and objectives, educational strategies, implementation, and evaluation and feedback — to blended learning curricula, using the online-adapted version by Chen et al. The adapted cycle "can serve as a helpful framework for the development of a blended learning course or curriculum, ensuring that no steps are omitted, and online and face-to-face phases are planned together and closely aligned". The authors most strongly recommend planning the revision early, since curriculum development often stops after evaluation instead of continuing the cycle of refining and improving.
requirements: A structured cycle so that steps are not omitted and online and face-to-face phases are planned together
Technological support for the implementation step and decisions about learning platforms when selecting educational strategies
constraints: For novel formats with no established local precedent, the authors state planning the revision phases is essential
target_learners: Healthcare profession students in a blended learning curriculum
target_learning_goals: Coherent curriculum design with aligned online and face-to-face phases
examples: The adapted Kern cycle includes step-specific aspects for online teaching, such as deciding about learning platforms when selecting suitable educational strategies
key_sources: Hege I, Tolks D, Adler M, Härtl A. (2020). Blended learning: ten tips on how to implement it into a curriculum in healthcare education. GMS Journal for Medical Education 37(5): Doc45. https://www.egms.de/en/journals/zma/2020-37/zma001338.shtml

article_title: Practical lessons for phone-based assessments of learning.
citation: Angrist N, Bergman P, Evans DK, Hares S, Jukes MCH, Letsomo T. (2020). Practical lessons for phone-based assessments of learning. BMJ Global Health. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjgh-2020-003030
title: Keep phone assessments short with simple instructions and practice items so they measure the target skill rather than language and test-taking skill
description: Phone administration bundles receptive language skills with the target skill, and without visual cues assessments become even more a test of vocabulary, listening and processing. The article advises simple instructions and practice items, and brief calls: general phone-survey guidance suggests 30 minutes, but assessments with young people should be shorter, with Botswana calls taking "between 15 and 20 min".
requirements: Simple instructions and practice items to focus the assessment on the target skill
Brief call and assessment length suited to crowded, interruption-prone home environments
constraints: Shorter assessments require larger samples to keep the same statistical precision across assessed students
Lengthy assessments may not be possible by phone
target_learners: Children and youth, particularly in low-income and middle-income settings with multiple languages
target_learning_goals: Valid measurement of numeracy and literacy skills by phone
examples: In Botswana, assessors sent word problems by text, read questions aloud in order of difficulty (addition through division), timed each question at a maximum of 2 minutes, and kept calls to 15–20 minutes, about half of which was assessment time.
key_sources: Angrist N, Bergman P, Evans DK, Hares S, Jukes MCH, Letsomo T. (2020). Practical lessons for phone-based assessments of learning. BMJ Global Health. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjgh-2020-003030

article_title: Virtual patients as a tool for training pre-registration pharmacists and increasing their preparedness to practice: A qualitative study.
citation: Thompson Jessica; White Simon; Chapman Stephen. (2020). Virtual patients as a tool for training pre-registration pharmacists and increasing their preparedness to practice: A qualitative study. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0238226
title: Three-dimensional virtual patient simulations with decision-tree database, 3D avatar and free-text input for pre-registration pharmacist training
description: The study's VP simulations simulate clinical scenarios in a three-dimensional environment with an avatar that responds to learner input. The article states the "VP software has three key parts associated with, and essential to its design: an electronic database containing the VPs responses, a computer generated graphic and a system linking the two together", using a decision tree to map case progress. Three cases (emergency hormonal contraception, renal function, childhood illness) combined multiple-choice and free-text input with animated verbal and textual individualised feedback.
requirements: Scripts designed to meet pre-defined learning objectives, created in consultation with registered pharmacists with relevant expertise
Free-text input requires a keyword database and web service to process user text and drive the animation
constraints: Free-text interaction is limited to a programmed set of questions, as the keyword database did not pick up all spellings, words or phrases
Some trainees experienced browser accessibility problems on smart devices
target_learners: pre-registration pharmacist trainees in UK hospital or community pharmacy
target_learning_goals: clinical scenario decision-making
communication and consultation skills
pharmacotherapy knowledge such as emergency hormonal contraception and renal function calculation
examples: EHC simulation used both multiple-choice and free-text input with an integrated consultation form
childhood illness simulation enlarged an image of the child's arm or showed the oral cavity in response to free-text requests
key_sources: Thompson Jessica; White Simon; Chapman Stephen. (2020). Virtual patients as a tool for training pre-registration pharmacists and increasing their preparedness to practice: A qualitative study. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0238226
